The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven for hours to reach the coast, and when we finally stepped onto the sand, the world felt different—bigger, louder, alive in a way I couldn’t explain. The waves crashed against the shore like they were trying to tell me something, but I didn’t understand the language yet. I remember crouching down, letting the water lap at my fingers, half-expecting it to pull me in. It didn’t. It just kept coming, relentless and gentle at the same time.

That moment stuck with me because it was the first time I felt small in the best way. The ocean didn’t care about my childhood worries—about school, or the way my socks always slipped into my shoes, or the quiet fear that I’d never be enough. It just was. And in its vastness, I found a strange kind of comfort.

Years later, I still go to the water when I need to remember that the world is bigger than my problems. Sometimes I sit on the beach and watch the horizon, wondering what’s out there beyond what I can see. Other times, I just listen to the waves, letting their rhythm drown out the noise in my head.

The ocean teaches me patience. It reminds me that things change—tides rise and fall, storms pass, and even the strongest waves eventually calm. And maybe that’s the lesson: to trust the process, to keep moving forward even when the current feels too strong. Because no matter how much I try to hold onto the shore, the ocean will always be there, pulling me back into its endless, restless heart.
